sections.title: Signs, adverts and recipes
sections.content: You know notices with *se prohíbe* from A2 Unit 24, and *se busca* and *se requiere* from B1 Unit 6. Notices, adverts and instructions use *se* because they speak to everybody and the doer does not matter. The rule you already know picks the verb: an infinitive or a noun for something uncountable (*silencio*) takes a singular verb, and a plural noun takes a plural verb. What is new here is how many everyday notices follow this pattern, and the polite *Se ruega*, which means "please".

items.spanish: Se pelan las patatas y se cortan en trozos.
items.english: The potatoes are peeled and cut into pieces.

items.spanish: Se agrega un poco de sal.

sections.content: A notice written as a command, such as *Guarde silencio*, speaks to you; you know *usted* commands from A2 Unit 23. A notice with *se* states a rule for everybody, so it sounds more formal and less personal. In a recipe the verb agrees with the ingredient: *se agrega sal*, *se agregan las patatas*.
